title: Mathematical Logic: Propositions, Quantifiers & Valid Arguments
description: The mathematics behind programming, computing, finance, business, and economics — one question at a time. Think it through, then choose A, B, or C, and move on at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of an existentially quantified statement over a finite domain.
questions.question: Let D = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and let P(x) be the predicate "x^2 is greater than 20." For at least one (some) x in D, is it true that P(x)? In symbols: ∃x ∈ D, P(x). Is this statement true or false?

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined without more information

questions.explanation: 5 ∈ D satisfies "x^2 is greater than 20" (a witness), so the existential statement is true. Since the domain D is finite and fully listed, the statement's truth value can always be determined by checking every element.
questions.hint: An existential statement is true as soon as you find even one witness that works.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the truth value of a compound proposition for a given truth assignment.
questions.question: Given P = False, Q = False, what is the truth value of ¬Q?

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined from the given information

questions.explanation: Substitute the given values into ¬Q and evaluate connective by connective following operator precedence (¬, then ∧/∨/⊕, then →, then ↔). This yields True. Since every variable's truth value is given, the result is always determined — it is never "cannot be determined."
questions.hint: Work from the innermost parentheses outward, applying NOT before AND/OR, and the conditional/biconditional last.

questions.concept: Forming the contrapositive of a conditional statement
questions.learningObjective: Given a conditional statement "If P, then Q," correctly form its contrapositive.
questions.question: Consider the statement: "If today is Saturday, then school is closed." What is its contrapositive?

options.label: A
options.text: If it is not the case that school is closed, then it is not the case that today is Saturday.

options.label: B
options.text: If school is closed, then today is Saturday.

options.label: C
options.text: If it is not the case that today is Saturday, then it is not the case that school is closed.

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of "If P, then Q" negates both parts and swaps their order to get "If not Q, then not P": "If it is not the case that school is closed, then it is not the case that today is Saturday."
questions.hint: Negate both parts, and also swap their order.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the proposition logically equivalent to a given expression using Idempotent Law.
questions.question: Which of the following is logically equivalent to P ∧ P?
questions.explanation: By Idempotent Law, P ∧ P is logically equivalent to P. This can be confirmed by checking that both sides have identical truth tables for every combination of P.
questions.hint: Think about which standard law of logic (De Morgan, double negation, contrapositive, distributive, absorption, ...) applies here.

questions.concept: Recognizing propositions and their truth value
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a declarative sentence is a proposition and, if so, evaluate its truth value.
questions.question: Consider the sentence: "7 is a prime number." Which of the following best describes it?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not a proposition — it has no single fixed truth value.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a proposition, and it is true.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a proposition, and it is false.

questions.explanation: A declarative sentence with a definite truth value is a proposition. 7 has no divisors other than 1 and itself, so it is prime; the sentence is therefore a true proposition.
questions.hint: First decide whether the sentence can be assigned exactly one of true/false — then check the arithmetic fact itself.

questions.concept: Classifying propositions as tautologies, contradictions, or contingencies
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a compound proposition is a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency.
questions.question: Consider the compound proposition P ↔ P. Which of the following correctly classifies it?

options.label: A
options.text: Contingency (true for some assignments, false for others)

options.label: B
options.text: Contradiction (always false, for every truth assignment)

options.label: C
options.text: Tautology (always true, for every truth assignment)

questions.explanation: Building the full truth table for P ↔ P over all combinations of its variables shows that it is true in every row, so it is a Tautology.
questions.hint: Try a couple of different truth assignments — if the value never changes, it's a tautology or contradiction; if it changes, it's a contingency.

options.label: A
options.text: It is a proposition, and it is true.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a proposition, and it is false.

options.label: C
options.text: It is not a proposition — it has no single fixed truth value.

questions.explanation: A declarative sentence with a definite truth value is a proposition. 45 can be divided evenly by a number other than 1 and itself, so it is not prime; the sentence is therefore a false proposition.
questions.hint: First decide whether the sentence can be assigned exactly one of true/false — then check the arithmetic fact itself.

questions.concept: Classifying propositions as tautologies, contradictions, or contingencies
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a compound proposition is a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency.
questions.question: Consider the compound proposition X ↔ X. Which of the following correctly classifies it?

options.label: A
options.text: Contingency (true for some assignments, false for others)

options.label: B
options.text: Contradiction (always false, for every truth assignment)

options.label: C
options.text: Tautology (always true, for every truth assignment)

questions.explanation: Building the full truth table for X ↔ X over all combinations of its variables shows that it is true in every row, so it is a Tautology.
questions.hint: Try a couple of different truth assignments — if the value never changes, it's a tautology or contradiction; if it changes, it's a contingency.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the number of rows needed in a truth table for a given number of propositional variables.
questions.question: A digital logic circuit's truth table is built from 2 distinct propositional (yes/no) variables. How many rows does its complete truth table need?
questions.explanation: Each of the 2 variables independently takes one of 2 values, so the number of rows needed to cover every combination is 2^2 = 4.
questions.hint: Each additional variable doubles the number of rows — the count is 2 raised to the power of the number of variables.

questions.explanation: The converse of "If P, then Q" swaps the antecedent and consequent to get "If Q, then P": "If it is isosceles, then a triangle is equilateral."

questions.question: Consider the statement: "If a integer n is even, then n^2 is even." What is its contrapositive?

options.label: A
options.text: If it is not the case that n^2 is even, then it is not the case that a integer n is even.

options.label: B
options.text: If n^2 is even, then a integer n is even.

options.label: C
options.text: If it is not the case that a integer n is even, then it is not the case that n^2 is even.

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of "If P, then Q" negates both parts and swaps their order to get "If not Q, then not P": "If it is not the case that n^2 is even, then it is not the case that a integer n is even."
questions.hint: Negate both parts, and also swap their order.

options.label: C

options.text: If it is not the case that it is raining, then it is not the case that the ground is wet.

options.label: B
options.text: If it is not the case that the ground is wet, then it is not the case that it is raining.

options.label: C
options.text: If the ground is wet, then it is raining.

questions.hint: Negate both parts, and also swap their order.

questions.concept: Translating English statements into symbolic logic
questions.learningObjective: Translate a compound English sentence into correct propositional-logic notation using the given atomic propositions.
questions.question: Let P: "She studies." and Q: "She passes." Translate the following sentence into symbolic notation: "She does not pass unless she studies."
questions.explanation: The sentence "She does not pass unless she studies." matches the symbolic form ¬P → ¬Q, using P and Q as defined and combining them with the connective(s) that mirror the sentence's structure.
questions.hint: Identify the connective words in the sentence (and, or, not, if...then, if and only if, unless, only if) and map each one to its symbol.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the truth value of a compound proposition for a given truth assignment.
questions.question: Given P = True, Q = False, R = True, what is the truth value of P ∨ (¬Q)?

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be determined from the given information

questions.explanation: Substitute the given values into P ∨ (¬Q) and evaluate connective by connective following operator precedence (¬, then ∧/∨/⊕, then →, then ↔). This yields True. Since every variable's truth value is given, the result is always determined — it is never "cannot be determined."
questions.hint: Work from the innermost parentheses outward, applying NOT before AND/OR, and the conditional/biconditional last.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of an existentially quantified statement over a finite domain.
questions.question: Let D = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} and let P(x) be the predicate "x is prime." For at least one (some) x in D, is it true that P(x)? In symbols: ∃x ∈ D, P(x). Is this statement true or false?

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot be determined without more information

questions.explanation: 2 ∈ D satisfies "x is prime" (a witness), so the existential statement is true. Since the domain D is finite and fully listed, the statement's truth value can always be determined by checking every element.
questions.hint: An existential statement is true as soon as you find even one witness that works.

questions.learningObjective: Identify Disjunctive Syllogism as the rule of inference used in a short argument.

questions.explanation: This argument has the form P ∨ Q, ¬P ⊢ Q, which is exactly the pattern of Disjunctive Syllogism.
questions.hint: Match the shape of the premises and conclusion to the standard inference-rule patterns (Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, syllogisms, simplification, etc.).

questions.concept: Classifying propositions as tautologies, contradictions, or contingencies
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a compound proposition is a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency.
questions.question: Consider the compound proposition (X ∨ Y) ∧ (¬Y). Which of the following correctly classifies it?

options.label: A
options.text: Contingency (true for some assignments, false for others)

options.label: B
options.text: Contradiction (always false, for every truth assignment)

options.label: C
options.text: Tautology (always true, for every truth assignment)

questions.explanation: Building the full truth table for (X ∨ Y) ∧ (¬Y) over all combinations of its variables shows that it is true in some rows and false in others, so it is a Contingency.
questions.hint: Try a couple of different truth assignments — if the value never changes, it's a tautology or contradiction; if it changes, it's a contingency.

questions.concept: Logical equivalence of a conditional and its contrapositive
questions.learningObjective: Recognize that a conditional statement is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, but not to its converse or inverse in general.
questions.question: Consider the statement: "If a polygon is a square, then it has four right angles." Which of the following is logically equivalent to it (guaranteed to have the same truth value in every case)?

options.label: A
options.text: If it is not the case that it has four right angles, then it is not the case that a polygon is a square.

options.label: B
options.text: If it is not the case that a polygon is a square, then it is not the case that it has four right angles.

options.label: C
options.text: If it has four right angles, then a polygon is a square.

questions.explanation: A conditional "If P, then Q" is logically equivalent only to its contrapositive, "If not Q, then not P": "If it is not the case that it has four right angles, then it is not the case that a polygon is a square." The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original statement, since swapping or negating just one part of an implication can change its truth value.
questions.hint: Only one of the three related forms (converse, inverse, contrapositive) always shares the same truth value as the original conditional.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the proposition logically equivalent to a given expression using Absorption Law.
questions.question: Which of the following is logically equivalent to P ∧ (P ∨ Q)?
questions.explanation: By Absorption Law, P ∧ (P ∨ Q) is logically equivalent to P. This can be confirmed by checking that both sides have identical truth tables for every combination of P, Q.
questions.hint: Think about which standard law of logic (De Morgan, double negation, contrapositive, distributive, absorption, ...) applies here.

questions.learningObjective: Correctly negate a universally or existentially quantified statement (moving the negation inside flips the quantifier).
questions.question: Let D = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} and let P(x) be the predicate "x is odd." What is the correct negation of the statement ∀x ∈ D, P(x)?
questions.explanation: The negation of a universal statement is an existential statement about the negated predicate: ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). So the negation of "∀x ∈ D, P(x)" is "∃x ∈ D, ¬P(x)."
questions.hint: Negating a quantified statement flips ∀ to ∃ (or ∃ to ∀) and negates the predicate — it does NOT just negate the predicate alone.

questions.concept: Classifying propositions as tautologies, contradictions, or contingencies
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a compound proposition is a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency.
questions.question: Consider the compound proposition (X ∧ Y) ∧ (¬X). Which of the following correctly classifies it?

options.label: A
options.text: Contradiction (always false, for every truth assignment)

options.label: B
options.text: Contingency (true for some assignments, false for others)

options.label: C
options.text: Tautology (always true, for every truth assignment)

questions.explanation: Building the full truth table for (X ∧ Y) ∧ (¬X) over all combinations of its variables shows that it is false in every row, so it is a Contradiction.
questions.hint: Try a couple of different truth assignments — if the value never changes, it's a tautology or contradiction; if it changes, it's a contingency.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the proposition logically equivalent to a given expression using Exportation Law.
questions.question: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (X ∧ Y) → Z?
questions.explanation: By Exportation Law, (X ∧ Y) → Z is logically equivalent to X → (Y → Z). This can be confirmed by checking that both sides have identical truth tables for every combination of X, Y, Z.
questions.hint: Think about which standard law of logic (De Morgan, double negation, contrapositive, distributive, absorption, ...) applies here.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the truth value of a compound proposition for a given truth assignment.
questions.question: Given P = True, Q = False, R = True, what is the truth value of (¬Q) ∧ ((¬P) ↔ Q)?

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined from the given information

questions.explanation: Substitute the given values into (¬Q) ∧ ((¬P) ↔ Q) and evaluate connective by connective following operator precedence (¬, then ∧/∨/⊕, then →, then ↔). This yields True. Since every variable's truth value is given, the result is always determined — it is never "cannot be determined."
questions.hint: Work from the innermost parentheses outward, applying NOT before AND/OR, and the conditional/biconditional last.

questions.learningObjective: Apply Disjunctive Syllogism to a set of premises to derive the logically valid conclusion.
questions.question: Given the premises: (1) You finish the assignment or you may go to the party. (2) It is not the case that you finish the assignment., using Disjunctive Syllogism, what can you validly conclude?

options.label: A
options.text: You may go to the party.

options.label: B
options.text: It is not the case that you may go to the party.

options.label: C
options.text: You finish the assignment or you may go to the party.

questions.explanation: Disjunctive Syllogism has the pattern P ∨ Q, ¬P ⊢ Q. Applying it to the given premises yields the conclusion: "You may go to the party."
questions.hint: Recall the exact pattern of Disjunctive Syllogism and match the premises to its two (or more) required forms.
